articles.title: My AI assistant kept saying "all tests pass". So I built a gate that checks.
articles.excerpt: If you code with AI assistants, you've probably seen this: the agent says "done, all tests pass", and then you find out the tests never ran, were skipped, or were quietly edited so they would pass. I…
articles.body: If you code with AI assistants, you've probably seen this: the agent says "done, all tests pass", and then you find out the tests never ran, were skipped, or were quietly edited so they would pass. I hit this often enough that I stopped trusting the claim and built a tool to check it: BuildProof . What it does BuildProof is a CLI that sits between the AI and your repo: Fail-closed test gate - a change is accepted only if the real test suite actually ran and passed. If anything is unclear, it counts as a failure, not a pass. Guard - detects tampering: weakened assertions, skipped tests, or test files edited to force a pass. Rollback - a rejected change is rolled back to the last good state. Signed certificates - every accepted run gets an ed25519-signed proof that anyone can verify.

articles.title: TUF Protects Updates Only When Clients Enforce Its State
articles.excerpt: TUF Protects Updates Only When Clients Enforce Its State The Update Framework, or TUF, treats a software repository as an adversarial environment. It does not assume that a mirror, CDN, or metadata ho…
articles.body: TUF Protects Updates Only When Clients Enforce Its State The Update Framework, or TUF, treats a software repository as an adversarial environment. It does not assume that a mirror, CDN, or metadata host will always return the newest or the intended file. The framework organizes signed metadata into roles, limits what each role can authorize, and defines checks that an updater must perform. Those checks matter because a repository compromise can produce an internally consistent but outdated or mismatched update set. TUF's security model names several attacks that a naive updater handles badly. A rollback attack presents an older version that may contain known vulnerabilities. A fast-forward attack inflates version numbers so later legitimate updates look like rollbacks.

articles.excerpt: Writing unit mocks and end-to-end integration tests for microservices is slow and brittle. Here is how Keploy automates test and mock generation directly from API traffic. If you’ve ever maintained a…
articles.body: Writing unit mocks and end-to-end integration tests for microservices is slow and brittle. Here is how Keploy automates test and mock generation directly from API traffic. If you’ve ever maintained a microservice with database calls, payment webhooks, or third-party APIs, you know the universal pain of integration testing: You spend days writing boilerplate mock data for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis. An external API payload changes slightly, and your mocks become stale. Your unit tests pass with flying colors, but your code breaks in production because mocks didn't mirror real-world behavior. Recently, I’ve been testing Keploy —an open-source, AI-native test generation platform designed to eliminate the friction of manual mock writing.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide.

articles.body: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release .

articles.body: Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain.

While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X". It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space . "Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die.

articles.title: See NASA's Artemis III astronauts meet Trump at the White House as they train for a critical 2027 moon lander test flight (photos)
articles.excerpt: The astronauts of NASA's Artemis III mission met with President Trump at the White House on Wednesday (Oct. 28), just as the Artemis II spaceflyers did six months ago.
articles.body: U.S. President Donald Trump just met another NASA Artemis crew. The astronauts of NASA's Artemis III mission visited the Oval Office on Thursday (Oct. 28) and posed for a few photos with the president. Their visit came nearly six months to the day after that of the Artemis II crew, who stopped by the White House on April 29 , 19 days after the end of their historic flight around the moon . President Trump talks to the Artemis III crew on Oct. 28, 2026. (Image credit: The White House) The Artemis III astronauts are NASA's Randy Bresnik (commander), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (mission specialists) and the European Space Agency 's Luca Parmitano (pilot). All four — plus backup crewmate Bob Hines of NASA, and agency chief Jared Isaacman — made the White House trip.
